name: Platysmaplasty (neck band surgery)
lead: Platysmaplasty is a cosmetic surgical procedure that tightens, repositions or supports the platysma, the thin sheet of muscle across the front of the neck, to smooth vertical neck bands and sharpen the line between jaw and neck. It is usually performed as part of a neck lift or facelift, often with removal of submental fat.[1][2][4][6][11]

For appearance, the aim is a cleaner cervicomental angle and a more defined jawline. Surgeons describe the aging neck as changing in several layers at once: skin loses elasticity, the platysma can separate and show as vertical bands, and fullness under the chin can come from fat or deeper structures beneath the muscle, so treatment is individualised.[11] In looksmaxxing communities it is grouped with hardmaxxing procedures aimed at a sharper jawline and neck.

Techniques include midline (medial) plication, lateral suspension, combined approaches, and the corset platysmaplasty described in 1990, in which the muscle halves are joined into a single sheet.[1][7][11] The literature consists mainly of surgeons' technique descriptions and case series, with a few comparative reports.

paras: Platysmaplasty modifies the platysma by tightening it at the midline, suspending it at the sides, resecting or cutting it, or suturing it in a corset-like pattern.[1][11] Wikipedia notes that neck ageing does not follow one pattern: collagen and elastin decline in the skin, the platysma can separate and show vertical banding, and fullness beneath the chin can originate beneath the muscle from subplatysmal fat, the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles or the submandibular glands.[11]

Limited-incision approaches combining submental lipectomy with platysmaplasty have been published.[6] Anatomical work has analysed platysma suspension during neck lift in a series of 30 cases.[9] A surgeon's 2014 update describes a neck-lift strategy aiming to control the size, shape and position of each neck feature, based on 38 years of experience and 522 consecutive procedures from 2004 to 2013.[4]

Reference descriptions group the approaches into medial platysmaplasty (the corset technique), done through an incision under the chin and bringing the muscle edges together in the midline; lateral platysmaplasty or platysmapexy, which supports the muscle at the sides, for example by fixing it near the sternocleidomastoid fascia or the earlobe region; and combined medial and lateral repair.[11] One paper comparing them reported that medial platysmaplasty was generally more effective than simple lateral pulling for several neck deformities, particularly a midline deformity.[11]

The corset technique was described in 1990 and discussed again in 1992 as a nontraditional method that moves the muscle mainly forward, joining the two halves with a long infolded midline seam supplemented by vertical pleats and sling sutures, without resecting or transecting muscle.[1][7] Its authors framed it as a response to persistent bands, submandibular gland bulges and contour irregularities seen after earlier methods.[1][7]

Other surgeons use different philosophies. One vertical neck-lifting procedure, an extended deep plane facelift, does not routinely use midline platysmal surgery because the authors say it works against vertical redraping.[12] Reviews also describe direct cervicoplasty or submentoplasty for patients whose concern is limited to loose neck skin and who do not want a full facelift, with the trade-offs of shorter operations and recovery but a visible anterior scar; a 2024 chapter addresses direct neck lift in men.[13][14] Deep neck techniques addressing subplatysmal fat, digastric muscle or submandibular gland are often combined with platysmaplasty when those structures contribute to fullness.[11] A 2020 review covers incorporating midline platysmaplasty with lateral SMAS facelifting.[15]

Reference text describes layered, tension-free closure after the muscle repair, with the platysma work carrying the structural support and the skin playing a secondary role.[11] Surgeons describe reliance on deep structural support rather than skin tension as aimed at longer-lasting definition of the cervicomental angle and fewer recurrent bands.[11]

Reported risks of platysmaplasty and neck lift include bleeding or hematoma, infection, numbness, temporary nerve weakness, contour problems and recurrent platysmal bands.[11] A review of 1078 consecutive facelifts examined factors associated with hematoma, described as the most common complication of rhytidectomy and a cause of prolonged swelling or skin necrosis.[2] Preliminary reports describe local infiltration of tranexamic acid to reduce intraoperative bleeding during facelifts, and a 2020 study examined local tranexamic acid for hemostasis in rhytidectomy.[3][16]

Surgery beneath the platysma adds structures to protect. Treating the submandibular glands has been associated with hematoma, saliva collections and weakness of nerves controlling the lower lip, and removing too much neck fat can create a hollow central contour sometimes called cobra neck, which is why fat removal is described as conservative.[11] Persistent or recurrent bands and visible gland bulges were the shortcomings that prompted the corset technique.[1]

Thread-lift sutures and barbed sutures have been reviewed as less invasive options in aesthetic surgery.[5][8] Platysmaplasty also appears in lower-face feminization surgery, where neck feminization may involve a tracheal shave, platysmaplasty or a deep neck procedure, alongside chin and jaw contouring.[17] A paired report of identical twins undergoing facelifts with different techniques gave a 10-year comparison.[10]

Neck definition features in hardmaxxing discussions as part of lower-face and jawline contour, often alongside chin, jaw implant and submental fat procedures. Online discussion treats it as a surgical option for people whose neck bands or slack obscure the jaw line, while surgeons' papers frame it mainly in the context of facial rejuvenation.

Evidence is largely retrospective case series and technique papers rather than randomized trials. Reported examples include a 1078-facelift hematoma review,[2] 522 neck lifts reviewed by one surgeon,[4] a 30-case anatomical analysis of platysma suspension,[9] and a 10-year twin comparison of two facelift techniques.[10] A systematic review of thread-lift sutures concerns a related, less invasive approach.[5] A 2020 preliminary report found local tranexamic acid helpful for reducing facelift bleeding.[3]

card.summary: Surgery that tightens the neck's platysma muscle to remove bands and sharpen the neck line; supported by surgical case series, not trials.
card.aka: Neck lift muscle tightening, corset platysmaplasty
card.note: Real surgery with hematoma and other operative risks; evidence is mostly surgeon case series.

quick.overview:
Platysmaplasty tightens or reshapes the platysma muscle in the neck to reduce vertical bands and improve contour. It is usually done within a neck lift or facelift.

The published evidence is mainly surgeons' technique papers and case series; no randomized trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons plicate, cut or suture the platysma, for example in a corset pattern, so the muscle sits flatter and tighter beneath the skin.
quick.risks: Hematoma is the most common complication of related facelift surgery; persistent bands and contour irregularities have been reported with some techniques. It is performed by surgeons under anesthesia.

chain: Surgeon tightens or repositions the platysma muscle
Vertical neck bands and slack are reduced
Cleaner jaw-neck line and cervicomental angle
angle.text: Platysmaplasty reshapes the muscle sheet under the chin so bands flatten and the neck meets the jaw at a sharper angle. People pursue it for neck contour and, in the looksmaxxing framing, a more defined lower face.
